subsystems.name: Micro-robot units
subsystems.role: the individual agents — centimetre-to-millimetre machines that move, sense and carry a small tool.
parts: mobility (legs, wheels, vibration or magnetic actuation)
sensors for cracks, corrosion and position

subsystems.name: Power
subsystems.role: keeping thousands of tiny robots alive without wires.

subsystems.name: Localisation and messaging
subsystems.role: each robot needs to know roughly where it is and to signal its neighbours locally.

subsystems.name: Coordination software
subsystems.role: no central controller — the swarm's behaviour emerges from simple local rules.
parts: stigmergy rules (robots alter the environment, others react)
ant-colony-style task allocation and path routing

subsystems.name: Repair payload
subsystems.role: the actual fixing: building up material where structure has been lost.

subsystems.name: Deployment and supervision
subsystems.role: getting the swarm onto a bridge or pipe, and keeping a human in the loop.
parts: inspection database and engineering review tools

buildSteps.title: Design the single robot
buildSteps.detail: Fix the size, locomotion and tool. At centimetre scale, wheels or vibration motors are practical; below that, engineers use magnetic fields, acoustic waves or MEMS actuators inspired by wafer-scale fabrication.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate thousands at once
buildSteps.detail: Instead of assembling each robot, units would be patterned in sheets using photolithography and printed-circuit techniques, then released and folded — the only credible route to millions.

buildSteps.title: Solve the power budget
buildSteps.detail: Fit the smallest battery that will run the motors and radio for a working shift, plus harvesting from vibration or light, or design docking stations where robots recharge before resuming.

buildSteps.title: Give each robot a voice
buildSteps.detail: Add a short-range radio or infrared link so a robot only talks to neighbours within a metre or so, and onboard sensing so it can tell sound material from cracked or corroded material.

buildSteps.title: Write the swarm rules
buildSteps.detail: Program simple local behaviours — follow a trace, deposit a trace, reinforce the strongest trail — so that ant-colony-inspired feedback routes more robots to the largest damage patch without any central command.

buildSteps.title: Simulate, then test in an arena
buildSteps.detail: Run tens of thousands of virtual agents first, then hundreds of real robots on a test slab to check that the emergent behaviour is stable and cannot run away.

buildSteps.title: Deploy onto the structure
buildSteps.detail: A carrier places the swarm on a bridge deck or into a pipe. A fixed beacon grid provides position, the robots fan out, and they collectively build a damage map of the asset.

buildSteps.title: Repair in many tiny passes
buildSteps.detail: Robots deposit small amounts of resin, mortar or coating and prepare the surface ahead of the next robot. No single robot does a meaningful repair; the swarm does it by accumulating thousands of passes over the same spot.

buildSteps.title: Verify and withdraw
buildSteps.detail: The swarm re-scans the repair and hands the data to a human engineer for sign-off, then returns to docking stations to recharge or is retrieved.

prerequisites.why: micro-robots have been built and steered in labs, but not manufactured in the millions or made to work outdoors for long.
batteries shrink far worse than motors and radios, so tiny robots run for minutes, not days.
ant-colony optimisation and stigmergy are well-established, and robot swarms of a few thousand have self-assembled in laboratories, but not in messy field conditions.
depositing material that genuinely restores structural strength is a job still done by people with scaffolding and mixers.
under a bridge or inside a pipe, satellites are useless; beacon networks and lidar work but are not yet small, cheap and robust enough for a disposable robot.

pathway.milestone: coordinated inspection fleets — drones flying survey patterns and crawler robots travelling inside pipes
pathway.unlocks: fast, repeatable condition mapping of large assets, with humans making the repair decisions.

pathway.milestone: swarms of tens to hundreds of robots doing simple building and clean-up tasks in controlled settings
pathway.unlocks: confidence that emergent behaviour is safe around people and property.

pathway.milestone: hybrid operations where a swarm inspects, tags and prepares a site and a larger robot or crew does the structural work
pathway.unlocks: real reductions in inspection cost and scaffolding time on bridges, dams and pipelines.

pathway.milestone: self-contained swarms that deposit material and cure it, with an engineer approving the result remotely
pathway.unlocks: routine autonomous patching of small defects before they become expensive failures.

pathway.milestone: millions of disposable robots permanently resident on critical infrastructure
pathway.unlocks: continuous, always-on maintenance — but only if micro-power, fabrication cost and reliability all improve by orders of magnitude.
